name: Byron as 'myth' versus Byron as he actually was
plain_explanation: Russell argues that Byron's world-historical importance rests less on his actual character or the literary quality of his poetry than on the simplified, larger-than-life image ('myth') the world made of him -- a despairing, sinning, freedom-loving Titan -- which was transmitted, developed, and transmuted abroad long after the real, more ambivalent and half-posing man had died.
precise_definition: Russell's distinction between Byron's actual, more ambivalent psychology (partly posed, partly sincere, sometimes privately preferring Pope's poetry to his own) and the simplified Continental 'myth' of Byron as heroic rebel-sinner, which Russell treats as the actually operative historical force, independent of its accuracy.
why_it_mattered: It licenses Russell's broader methodological point that a historian of philosophy assessing influence must sometimes attend to a figure's mythic reception rather than their literal biography or literary merit.
historical_origin: Drawn from Russell's own comparative reading of Byron's English versus Continental reception.
examples: French newspapers, on Byron's death, calling Napoleon and Byron 'the two greatest men of the century'
Byron's romanticism being 'only half sincere,' since he privately sometimes judged Pope's poetry superior to his own
influence_on_later_thinkers: Explains why Byron's 'spiritual progeny' is to be sought abroad (in Musset, Heine, and eventually Nietzsche) rather than in England.
